text: Before the word work, here’s a little secret. Long words are often built from smaller pieces, the way a castle is built from stones. Today you’ll find two of those pieces and figure out what each one means, before the page tells you. After that come some joining words and some vowel pairs. Take it one step at a time.

Before you open the book: Chapter 1 has a feast, a prank, and a boy in a cold tower. As you read, keep asking yourself who gives the orders, and who has to obey. And listen to how Jemmy talks. He grew up on the city streets, and the author wants you to hear it.

Now it’s your turn to have an opinion. A good claim names a character, says what you think of them, and hints at why. You can pick any character, as long as the book gives you a reason. Think back over the feast and the lessons. Then write your claim in one strong sentence.
Jemmy talks like the streets he grew up on. Words like ain’t and me rags aren’t mistakes. The author wrote them on purpose so you can hear Jemmy in your head. Tap each one to find out what it means.

This little prince was real. His name was Edward, and he lived in England about five hundred years ago. Stories say a friend of his took his punishments, but nobody knows if that’s true. In our book, it’s the rule, and Jemmy is the one who pays.
Contrite. The prince lowered his head so as to appear humbled and contrite. Contrite means truly sorry for something you did wrong. The prince is only pretending.
Defiantly. Defiantly biting back every yelp and cry, the whipping boy received the twenty whacks. Defiantly means boldly refusing to give in. Jemmy won't cry, because that's what the prince wants.
Exasperation. Listen to the sentence. But all the while he was feeling a growing exasperation with his whipping boy. Exasperation means a strong feeling of being fed up.
Forbidden. And it was forbidden to spank, thrash, cuff, smack, or whip a prince. Forbidden means not allowed. It's against the rules.

Now show what you understood. A good answer does two things. It's a full sentence, and it has a detail from the book. So don't just write, he played a prank. Tell what the prank was. Here are your questions. One, what prank did the prince play at the feast, and what did the guests do? Two, why does the prince call Jemmy the worst whipping boy ever? Three, what does Jemmy secretly hope for, and does it happen? Want a challenge? Pick Scholar, and add one more detail to each answer.

[warmly] This is copia. It means saying one idea in many ways, and it makes you a stronger writer. Watch me try one first, with a different sentence. Jemmy swept the floor. Box one, change the opener: In the cold tower, Jemmy swept the floor. Box two, swap the verb for a stronger one: Jemmy scrubbed the floor. Box three, add a where or a how: Jemmy swept the floor slowly, humming to himself. Same idea, three new ways. Now you try with the king's sentence. Use your own words, not mine.

Let's fix a sentence. First, look at the correct one at the top. Someone is talking, so the words they say go inside quotation marks. The first word they say gets a capital letter. The king is shouting, so an exclamation mark goes inside the closing quotation mark. Tap the yellow parts to see each rule. Then pick Sentence A or Sentence B, and type it the right way. Look back at the model whenever you need to.

Some little words do a big job. And, but, and so are joining words. They glue two ideas into one sentence. And adds one more idea: I'm hungry and I'm tired. But shows a difference: I'm hungry, but there's no food. So shows what happens next: I'm hungry, so I'll eat. Find the joining word in Jemmy's sentence. Then tap each sentence and drop it in and, but, or so. Say it out loud with each word to hear which one fits.

Long words are often built from smaller parts, like a castle is built from stones. Today's parts are inter and sub. Think of the internet. It connects computers between each other. Now think of a subway. It's a train that runs under the city. So inter means between, and sub means under. Tap See what each part means to check. Then put the parts together, and type each whole word.

Time to read Chapters 1 and 2 in your book. Before you start, read the two Pause and Think questions below. They tell you where to stop. Watch for the moment the king shouts, Fetch the whipping boy, and ask yourself why the prince never worries about getting punished. In Chapter 2, watch the prince's lesson. Who is really learning? When you reach each question, stop, think of your answer, and keep reading.

Some vowels like to work in pairs. When two vowels sit side by side in one beat and make one sound, we call them a vowel team. In feast, the e and the a team up to say ee. In groan, the o and the a say oh. Say each word out loud and clap the beats. Then tap Now name the pattern. Last, sort the words. Two vowels side by side? That's a team.

Let's think about Jemmy for a moment. He didn't ask for this job. He was taken off the streets and brought to the castle, just to be punished for someone else. When the prince plays a prank, Jemmy gets twenty whacks, and he doesn't make a sound. Why would he stay quiet? Keep that question in mind as you read.

When you meet a word you don't know, don't skip it. Be a word detective. Let's try exasperation. First, read the sentence around it. The prince is pretending to be sorry, but inside, something is building up toward Jemmy. Next, look at the parts. Asper means rough. So exasperation is a rough, fed-up feeling, like when someone won't stop poking you. Now tap Opti reads it on each card, guess what the word means, and flip the card to check. Then play the matching game.

[warmly] Here's a trick good readers use. They ask, who's in charge here? This book has a king, a spoiled prince, and a boy named Jemmy who has no power at all. Below are two lenses. One asks, who gives the orders? The other asks, who gets what? Tap the one you will use while you read. You don't need to write anything.

Today you'll write a claim. A claim is your opinion, said clearly, with a reason. Meet Clara. Her first idea was, I think the prince is bad. That's a start, but bad doesn't tell us much. So Clara made it stronger: Prince Brat is the most unfair character, because he uses his power to hurt others. See the three parts? A character. What she thinks. And a reason why. Now it's your turn. Pick a character, say what you think, and tell us why.

Hello again, it’s Opti. Today we open a brand-new book, The Whipping Boy. Here’s something to think about: what if you got in trouble every time someone else broke a rule? Hold on to that question. First you’ll warm up your words, then you’ll read the first two chapters, and at the end you’ll decide what you think of the prince.

Word work first. Today you’ll match some long words to what they mean, and you’ll go hunting for joining words inside sentences. A joining word never comes alone. It brings a whole chunk of the sentence along with it. See if you can catch the word and its chunk together.

Before you read: the castle is about to disappear behind you. Chapter 3 happens at night, and Chapter 4 happens in a thick fog. Watch Jemmy closely. He’s thinking hard the whole time, even when he’s quiet. And keep an eye out for a glowing light.

Yesterday you wrote a claim. Today you give it a reason, the because behind your opinion. A strong reason comes from something a character really did, not just how you feel. Look back at today’s chapters and pick the one moment that proves your point best.
Astonishment. Jemmy stared at him with dreadful astonishment. Astonishment means a feeling of great surprise or shock.
Cutthroat. A cutthroat! he thought. A cutthroat is a dangerous criminal who would do anything for money.
Gallows. More likely I'll be hung from the gallows. A gallows is a wooden frame that was used long ago to punish people by hanging. Jemmy is afraid of a terrible punishment.
Strayed. A thick fog had swirled in, they'd strayed from the road, and trees had closed in on them. Strayed means wandered off the path by mistake.

Now show what you understood. Remember, a good answer is a full sentence with a detail from the book. One, what is Jemmy's plan to escape in the fog, and what stops it? Two, when the strangers grab the boys, what does Jemmy think they are, and why is he scared? Three, why does the prince pick Jemmy to run away with? Use a detail from Chapter 3. Want a challenge? Pick Scholar, and add one more detail to each answer.

Let's fix a sentence. Look at the correct one first. The prince is talking, so his words go inside quotation marks. A comma goes before the closing quotation mark, because the sentence keeps going: the prince announced to Jemmy. Tap the yellow parts to see each rule. Then pick Sentence A or Sentence B. Add the quotation marks, the comma, and the capital letters, and type it the right way.

Joining words are back, and today you're a joining-word spotter. In each sentence, first tap the joining word. Then tap the part of the sentence that comes after it. That part is the new idea the joining word brings in. Last, pick one sentence and write it again with a different joining word. Notice how the meaning changes.

When you see a long word, find the part at the start first, then read the rest. Tap a word in the game, then tap what it means. If you're stuck, look at the first part of the word. It gives you a big clue.

This is a haiku, a tiny poem with a fixed shape. The first line has five beats, the second has seven, and the last has five again. A haiku holds one picture and doesn't explain it. Read all three out loud. Then go back to the first one and clap each beat. Snow, on, the, court, yard. That's five! Keep clapping, and check that you get five, seven, five.

Time to read Chapters 3 and 4 in your book. First, read the two Pause and Think questions below, so you know where to stop. In Chapter 3, look for the prince's real reason for running away. In Chapter 4, a thick fog rolls in and two strangers appear. Ask yourself who Jemmy thinks they are, and why he's so scared. Stop at each question, think of your answer, and keep reading.

[warmly] Here's how Read Like a Writer works. I'll do one first, with a different sentence from Chapter 4. Like a snake striking, a ghostly hand darted through the fog and clutched his arm. Part one, read like a reader. What is happening? Someone in the fog grabs Jemmy, fast. Part two, read like a writer. What is the author doing? He says the hand moves like a snake striking, so we feel how quick and scary it is. Part three, mimic. Here's mine: Like a cat pouncing, my little sister grabbed the last cookie. Now it's your turn with the fog sentence. Write one sentence in each box.

Let's go hunting for vowel teams. Read the two sentences slowly. Every time you see two vowels working together, tap that word. There's more than one, so keep looking until the game says you found them all.

Here's something to think about. The prince runs away for one reason: he's bored. Jemmy doesn't get a choice. He has to come along and carry the basket. But out in the fog, there are no guards and no castle walls. Watch Jemmy closely. He may see a chance of his own. Who do you think is really in charge out there?

Let's be word detectives again. Here's astonishment. Read the sentence: Jemmy stared at him with dreadful astonishment. Jemmy just heard something he never expected. Now look at the parts. Astonish means to surprise, and ment turns it into a thing. So astonishment is a feeling of great surprise.

[warmly] Here's today's reading tip. Good readers notice when a character makes a bad choice, and then watch what that choice causes. Today the prince decides to run away, and Jemmy has to go with him. As you read, ask yourself: whose idea was this, and whose fault is the trouble that follows? Then tap one of the two lenses below, and use it while you read. You don't need to write anything.

On Day 1 you wrote a claim. Today you'll give it a reason. A reason tells why your claim is true. Listen to Clara. Her claim was, Prince Brat is the most unfair character. Then she added, One reason is that Prince Brat wants Jemmy whipped hard for things the prince did. See how the reason backs up the claim? Copy your claim from Day 1 into the box. Then write one reason under it. You can start with, One reason is that.

Hi, it’s Opti. Last time you met a prince who never gets punished and a boy who always does. Today the prince has a big idea, and it isn’t a good one. As you read, ask yourself: is being bored a good enough reason to drag someone else into danger? Then you’ll give your opinion a reason to stand on.

Today the word work asks you to use what you’ve learned. You’ll build words from their parts, fill in sentences with this week’s vocabulary, and join short sentences with the right joining word. Before you type, read each sentence in your head. Your ears often know the answer before your eyes do.

Before you read Chapter 5, a tip: notice the moment Jemmy uses his elbow instead of his voice. Authors often show what a character is thinking through what they do. And when the lantern comes close to the saddle, slow down. One small thing changes everything.

Today your opinion gets proof. A text example is a moment from the book that shows your reason is true, and you always say which chapter it came from. Go back to a chapter, find the moment, and tell what happened in your own words.

Look closely at a king’s things, and you’ll often find his family’s signs, like lions and crowns. When the outlaws spot the king’s crest on the saddle, they know where that horse came from. Now it’s your turn. Design a crest that tells the world something about you.

Now show what you understood, in full sentences with details from the book. One, how does Jemmy know who Hold-Your-Nose Billy is, and what does that tell us about how famous Billy is? Two, when the prince says who he is, the outlaws don't bow. What do they do instead? Three, Jemmy jabbed the prince to keep him quiet. Was that the right thing to do? Use a detail to back up your answer. For a challenge, pick Scholar and add one more detail.

Let's fix a sentence about the outlaws. Look at the correct one first. Billy gets a capital letter, because it's a name. Commas go around the describing part in the middle: raw as a skinned ox. And a comma goes before and, because and joins two ideas. Tap the yellow parts to see each rule. Then pick Sentence A or B, and type it with capitals, commas, and a period.

Today you'll do the joining yourself. Each pair has two short sentences. Glue them into one with and, but, or so. Ask yourself: am I adding an idea? Use and. Are the two ideas different, or surprising? Use but. Does the first thing cause the second? Use so. Read each one out loud with the word you picked. Then tap Check My Answers, and write your own sentence about Chapter 5 that uses but.

Today you'll build words from their parts. Remember, inter means between, and sub means under. Say each pair of parts out loud, then say them together as one word. Inter, rupt: interrupt. Hear how the parts snap together? Type the whole word in each box, then tap Check My Answers. Look at the little meaning next to each one. It tells you what you just built.

Time to read Chapter 5. First, read the two Pause and Think questions below. In this chapter, Jemmy jabs the prince with his elbow. Ask yourself why. Then watch the outlaw named Cutwater. He notices something on the saddle that changes everything. Stop at each question, think of your answer, and keep reading. After you read, try the King's Crest to see what Cutwater saw.

Here's today's rule: when you split a word into syllables, never split the team. The team always stays together. Rain, bow. Sea, son. Look at each word, find the vowel team, and think about where the split goes. Then tap the word to check.

Think about this before you read. When two outlaws grab the boys, the prince keeps telling them who he is. Jemmy tries to stop him without saying a word. Why would Jemmy want the prince to stay quiet? What might happen if outlaws find out they have a prince? Watch who keeps his head, and who keeps talking.

Here's a word from Chapter 5: ruffian. The prince calls Billy a clod and a ruffian. He's insulting him, so a ruffian must be someone rough and rude. Ruffian has no parts to help, so the sentence does the work. A ruffian is a rough, violent person, a bully. Now the other words in the word bank. An exploit is a bold, daring act. An heir is the person who will be king one day. And a ransom is money demanded to set a prisoner free. Fill in each sentence, then tap Check My Work.

[warmly] Here's today's reading tip. Good readers notice what a character does when he's in danger. In Chapter 5, two outlaws grab the boys. Watch Jemmy. Does he fight, does he try to trick them, or does he stay quiet? And think about why he makes that choice. Then tap one of the two lenses below to use while you read. You don't need to write anything.

You have a claim and a reason. Today you'll prove your reason with an example from the book. Clara's reason was, Prince Brat enjoys watching Jemmy get whipped. To prove it, she found a real moment. For example, in Chapter 2, the prince tells the tutor, ten whacks at least. Always name the chapter, so your reader can find it. Now write one example of your own. Start with, For example, in Chapter. Then copy it into your document.

Hello, it’s Opti. Our runaways are in real trouble now. Two rough men have found them in the fog, and one of the boys can’t seem to stop talking. Today, think about this: when you’re in danger, is it smarter to stay quiet or to speak up? Watch what each boy chooses.

Word study review day. You’ll roll some dice, fix joining words that don’t fit, and fill in sentences with words from all week. When something feels tricky, think back to Day 1. The patterns haven’t changed. You’ve just gotten better at spotting them.

No new chapters today. Instead, think back over the whole story so far. Picture the feast, the tower, the fog, and the outlaws. Which moment tells you the most about the prince? Which one tells you the most about Jemmy? Keep those two moments in mind.

Time to be your own editor. Read your claim, your reason, and your example out loud. Does each part do its job? Does your example really prove your reason? Find one thing to make stronger. Even great writers fix their work before anyone else reads it.

Now look back and answer in full sentences, with details from the book. One, describe Jemmy's life at the castle. What is good about it, and what is hard? Two, what are two pranks the prince has pulled, and why does no one ever punish him? Three, both boys are captives now. Who is more responsible for that? Use one detail. For a challenge, pick Scholar, and add one more detail to each answer.

Let's fix a sentence. Look at the correct one. The prince says one word: Boring. That word goes inside quotation marks, and it starts with a capital letter. A comma comes right before the opening quotation mark, after the word said. And the period goes inside the closing quotation mark. Tap the yellow parts to see each rule. Then pick Sentence A or B, and type it the right way.

Today you're the teacher, checking someone else's work. Some of these sentences use the wrong joining word. Read each sentence out loud. If the joining word doesn't match the meaning, tap it. If the sentence is right, tap No mistake. Then tell which sentence had no mistake, and how you knew.

Let's play with inter and sub one more time. Before you roll, say it out loud: inter means between, sub means under. Tap Roll the Dice. When a word comes up, find its first part, and say what the whole word means. Then tap Check My Thinking to see if you were right. Keep rolling until you've done all six words.

Here are the three haiku again. Remember, a haiku holds one small picture and doesn't explain it. Today, you get to choose. Read all three out loud, and pick the one you like best. Then close your eyes and see the picture it puts in your head. Is it the snow, the rat with the candles, or the soup that no one eats? Say your picture out loud. You don't need to write it.

There are no new chapters today. Instead, look back through Chapters 1 to 5 in your book. First, read the two Pause and Think questions below. One asks about the biggest conflict: which characters are against each other, and over what? The other asks you to predict. What will the outlaws do with a real prince? Flip back through the pages to find clues. You don't need to write these answers.

Let's roll some vowel team words. Tap Roll the dice. When a word comes up, say it out loud and clap the syllables. Find the vowel team, and remember, the team never splits. Meadow: mead, ow. Then tap Check my answer to see if you split it the right way.

Think about the two boys side by side. One has velvet clothes, a tutor, and a king for a father. The other has rags and a rat-catcher's know-how. But Jemmy also learned all the lessons the prince never did. Now they're both stuck with the same outlaws. Which boy do you think will be better at getting out of trouble?

This week you met lots of new words. Today you'll use four of them. Let's start with contrite. The prince lowered his head so as to appear humbled and contrite. He's trying to look sorry. So contrite means truly sorry for something you did wrong. Fill in each sentence from the word bank, then tap Check My Work.

[warmly] There are no new chapters today. Instead, good readers look back over everything they've read. Think about both boys in Chapters 1 to 5. The prince has velvet clothes and a king for a father. Jemmy has rags, and he gets whipped for the prince's pranks. Which boy has the harder life? Do you feel sorry for either one? Think about why. Then tap one of the two lenses below to use while you look back. You don't need to write anything.

This week you wrote a claim, a reason, and an example. Today you'll check your work, like a real writer. Clara read her draft and asked three questions. Is my claim clear? Does my reason tell why? Is my example from the book? Then she found one thing to add. Now read your own claim, reason, and example. Ask the same three questions. Then write one thing you'll add or fix to make your opinion stronger.

Welcome back, it’s Opti. Today we look back at all five chapters. One boy has fine clothes and a king for a father. The other has rags and a lot of whacks. So here’s the big question: who really has the harder life? Hold on to your answer, because today you’ll check your whole opinion from top to bottom.

Hi, it’s Opti. This week’s passage is the very first page of The Whipping Boy. Read it three times. The first time, just get the words right. The second time, make it smooth. The third time, let your voice have fun with the prank. It really does get easier each time.

This week's sentences are compound sentences. A compound sentence is two complete thoughts, glued together with a comma and a joining word, like and, but, or so. Read the sentence from the book in the box. Could each half stand alone as its own sentence? Think about it, then tap Now check your thinking. Next, sort the word groups. Some are one thought. Some are two thoughts joined. And some are not sentences at all, because they leave you hanging. Tap a word group, then tap its column.

Let's crack a word part. Here are four words: transport, import, export, report. Say them out loud. What part do all four words share? Now think about each word. In every one, something is being moved from one place to another. So what do you think that shared part means? Think of your answer. Then tap See if you cracked it to check. After that, type the missing root in each box, and tap Check My Work.

Say these words out loud: table, little, candle, simple. Listen to the last beat of each word. Now look at the last three letters, and look where the dot goes. What do you notice? Tap See the Rule to check your idea. Then tap each of the eight words, and tap the group it belongs in. Watch out! Not every word ends the same way.

Let's be word detectives. Here's scheme. Read the sentence: A scheme had leaped into his head. Jemmy just thought of something, all of a sudden. Scheme has no prefix or suffix, so the sentence does the work. Something that leaps into your head when you're in trouble is probably a plan. A scheme is a clever plan, often a sneaky one. Now tap Opti reads it on each card. Guess the meaning, then flip the card to check. Then play the matching game.

Here's one to take apart. The fog rolled in, and the boys got lost. First thought: the fog rolled in. Second thought: the boys got lost. The word and is just the glue, so skip it. In each sentence, tap the first thought, then the second.

Watch this. Support. Find port at the end. Now look at the part in front: sup, which means under. So to support something is to carry it from underneath, like holding up a heavy box. Use the same trick on each word. Tap a word, then tap what it means.

[warmly] Read Like a Writer has three parts. Let me show you with a different sentence from Chapter 9. Cutwater yanked Jemmy to his feet. Part one, read like a reader. What is happening? Cutwater is angry, so he pulls Jemmy up, hard. Part two, read like a writer. Which word does the work? Yanked. The author could have said pulled, but yanked is stronger, so we feel how rough Cutwater is. Part three, mimic. Now I write my own: My little brother yanked the blanket off my bed. Now it's your turn with the prince's sentence. Write one sentence in each box.

Quick test. Cattle, kitten, carpet. Which one ends with a consonant and l, e? Say them. Cat, tle. That's the one. In each row, only one word ends that way. Say every word, listen to the last beat, and tap it.

Here's a word Billy uses: obliged. He tells the prince his father will be ever so much obliged. Billy is pretending to be polite. Obliged means thankful. The cards work just like last time: listen, guess, then flip. Then match all four.

These sentences lost their commas. Listen. The horse was fast, but the outlaws were faster. Hear the little pause after fast? The comma goes there, right before but. Find that spot in each sentence and type the word that comes just before it.

Let's build a silly one first. Tele means far. Tele, plus port. Teleport! To carry something far away in a flash. Now you build the real ones. Say each pair of parts out loud. Type the whole word in the box. Then tap Check My Answers.

Two tiles, one word. Pud, dle. Puddle! The d sticks with the l, e. Build each word the same way. Tap the first part, then the last part. If a tile is in the wrong spot, it won't stick, so try the other one.

Cutwater shouts, I'll whip the mulishness out of him! Mule, ish, ness: stubborn like a mule. Defiant, parley and contrary are in the word bank too. Read each sentence, try each word in the blank, and keep the one that makes sense. Then tap Check My Work.

Can you spot what's wrong? The fog was thick but, they kept going. The comma jumped to the wrong side of but! It belongs right before it. Read each sentence. Tap the word where the mistake is, or tap No mistake if it's right.

Roll it, then crack it. Every word on the dice has port in it, so you already know half the meaning. Look at the part in front of port. That part is your clue. Say what the whole word means out loud, then tap Check My Thinking. Do all six.

Here's how to split one. Bottle. Count back three letters from the end: t, l, e. Bot, tle. That's the split. Tap Roll the dice. Say the word out loud and split it into syllables. Then tap Check my answer. Roll all six words.

Last chance with this week's words: fathom, flummox, parley, and angling. Here's a trick. Read each sentence out loud with the word in the blank. If it sounds right and makes sense, keep it. Then tap Check My Work.
Bewildered. Hold-Your-Nose Billy's red eyebrows shot up in bewildered surprise. Bewildered means completely confused.
Ransom. The outlaws want gold from the king before they let the prince go. That gold is a ransom.
Trifle. That crown! A trifle, scoffed Hold-Your-Nose Billy. A trifle is a small thing that is not worth much. Billy thinks a golden crown is not enough!
Truss. Lads, you won't mind if I truss you up like a Christmas goose. To truss someone means to tie them up tight. That's Cutwater, in Chapter 12.

Two sentences. Leaves crackled. Leaves crackled under Jemmy's feet. What did the second one add? It tells you more about the leaves, and it starts with the little word under. Under is a preposition. It sits in front of a noun and ties it to the rest of the sentence. Some prepositions tell where. Some tell when. Some tell how. Tap Now check your thinking. Then tap each phrase, and tap the question it answers.

Here's a puzzle. Inspect. Spectator. Respect. Say them out loud. What five letters hide inside all three? Now picture a spectator at a ball game. What is a spectator doing the whole time? Watching! So what could that hidden part mean? Tap See if you were right. Then type the missing part in each box. Careful with suspect and expect. Say them slowly and listen for the s.

Clap this one with me. Im, por, tant. Three beats! A long word is just small chunks stacked up. Find the vowels, split between them, read each chunk, then push them together. Say the words in Group A and Group B, and clap them. Tap See the Rule. Then sort the six words. Look at each chunk. Does one end with a vowel, like ba in bacon? Or end with a silent e, like cake?

Let's be word detectives. Back in Chapter 8, Billy's red eyebrows shot up in bewildered surprise. Jemmy had just shocked him. Now the parts: be, wilder, e d. Wilder is an old word for getting lost in a wild place. So bewildered means so confused you feel lost. Now tap Opti reads it on each card. Guess, then flip. Then play the matching game.
Bramble. Brambles, reaching out like cat's claws, tore at their fine garments. A bramble is a prickly, thorny bush.
Foliage. Jemmy turned to the right and beat his way back into the foliage. Foliage means the leaves and branches of plants.
Instinct. A thoroughbred of the streets, Jemmy acted on instinct. Instinct is doing something without stopping to think.
Tilt. Jemmy covered the ground at full tilt. At full tilt means as fast as you can go.

Sentences love prepositions. Listen. The prince ran across the clearing to the edge of the woods. Across. To. Of. Three! Tap Check yourself. Then tap every preposition in each sentence. Keep going until you find them all.

Quick reminder: spect means look. Now try a new one. Spectacular. Find spect. The fireworks were spectacular. So amazing that everybody had to look! Do the same with each word on the left. Find spect, look at the parts around it, then tap the meaning that fits.

[warmly] Read Like a Writer has three parts. Let me show you with a different sentence, from Chapter 14. Brambles, reaching out like cat's claws, tore at their fine garments. Part one, read like a reader. What is happening? The boys push through thorny bushes, and the thorns rip their fancy clothes. Part two, read like a writer. What does the author do? He says the brambles are like cat's claws, so we can almost feel the scratch. Part three, mimic. Here's mine: The snow, stinging like tiny bees, bit at my cheeks. Now it's your turn with the chase sentence. Write one sentence in each box.
Clap this word: ham, bur, ger. Hamburger. Three beats! In each row, three words have two beats, and one word has three. Clap every word out loud, then tap the one with three beats.

Here's a bonus. Say these two words: cat, and city. Both start with c. But they don't sound the same! The letter after the c is the clue. When c or g comes right before e, i, or y, it goes soft.
